title: Something has happened
lede: If something has already gone wrong, this page is the fastest route to the right help. Take a breath first. You have more time than it feels like, and the things that matter most take about five minutes.
provenance: The advice on this page is the same in every country. It is what child protection agencies in the US, UK, Canada and Ireland all tell parents, and where they differ we say so. Only the reporting routes change depending on where you are, and those are set by the country you picked above.

steps.title: Stay calm, and say out loud that they are not in trouble
steps.body: Your reaction in the first minute decides how much they tell you in the next hour. Say it plainly: you are not in trouble, and I am going to help. Whatever choice they made, what has been done to them is the crime.

steps.title: Do not delete anything
steps.body: Block the person, but leave the messages, the images and the account exactly where they are. Deleting destroys what investigators need to identify them. If you want the account gone, deactivate it rather than deleting it, because deactivated data can still be recovered.

steps.title: Screenshot before you block
steps.body: Capture the conversation, the profile and anything they sent. Then block. Doing it in that order costs two extra minutes and is the difference between a report that goes somewhere and one that doesn't.

evidence.title: What to save before you block
evidence.intro: The first four are what an investigator will ask you for. The last two are SafeStart's own advice, and they make a report much easier to act on.
official: The messages themselves, including anything already deleted from view
Any images or videos that were sent or received
Phone numbers, and bank or payment details if money was asked for
The web addresses of any page where images have been shared
practical: The exact username, display name and profile link, which change often
Dates and times, or a screenshot that shows them
evidence.note: Save screenshots somewhere outside the app itself, so a deleted account doesn't take them with it. Your own photo library or an email to yourself is fine.

situations.label: Someone is threatening to share nude images
situations.summary: Sometimes called sextortion. Someone has an intimate image of your child, or claims to, and is demanding money or more images.

keyAdvice.title: Do not pay
keyAdvice.body: Paying almost never stops it. Offenders frequently share the material anyway, and once you have shown you can pay, they come back for more.

keyAdvice.title: If you have already paid, stop there
keyAdvice.body: Don't panic, and don't pay anything more. Paying once has not made things worse. Paying again will.

keyAdvice.title: Block, but keep everything
keyAdvice.body: Block them, and do not delete the profile or the messages. Those are what let investigators find the person behind the account.

keyAdvice.title: Tell your child this is not their fault
keyAdvice.body: Say it directly: the blackmailer is to blame, not you. Even if you made a choice you regret, what they are doing is a crime. And make clear your first move is to help, always.

situations.context: Financial sextortion targets teenage boys disproportionately. Where the victim's gender was recorded, around 83% were male, and boys aged roughly 14 to 17 are the most commonly targeted group. Victims as young as 8 have been reported, of both genders, so if you have a daughter this still applies to her.
situations.sources: Canadian Centre for Child Protection, UK National Crime Agency, FBI

situations.label: An adult has been contacting my child
situations.summary: Someone older has been messaging your child, and it has moved somewhere private, or turned sexual, or they have asked to meet.

keyAdvice.title: Report to the national body, not just the platform
keyAdvice.body: A platform report gets the account removed. A report to your country's child protection body is what gets the person investigated. Do both, and do the national one first. The reporting section above has the right one for where you are.

keyAdvice.title: Keep the account open for now
keyAdvice.body: Your instinct will be to delete the app. Preserve it until you have reported, then decide. A deleted account takes the evidence with it.

keyAdvice.title: Ask gently, and ask once
keyAdvice.body: You need to know roughly what happened and how long it has been going on. You do not need every detail, and pressing for detail is what makes children stop talking. The people who take your report are trained for that conversation.

situations.context: A common pattern is that contact starts inside a game or a public server and moves quickly to a private app. If your child has been asked to move a conversation somewhere more private, that on its own is worth reporting.

situations.label: An image of my child is being shared
situations.summary: A nude or sexual image of your child, taken when they were under 18, is circulating or has been posted.

keyAdvice.title: Use Take It Down, and know that StopNCII will turn you away
keyAdvice.body: Take It Down is a free removal service for images taken of someone under 18, and it works anywhere in the world. StopNCII is the adult equivalent and requires the person to have been 18 or over both when the image was taken and now, so it will reject a case involving a child. Parents land on the wrong one all the time.

keyAdvice.title: The image never leaves your device
keyAdvice.body: Take It Down turns the image into a digital fingerprint on your own device. The image itself is never uploaded anywhere. Participating platforms match that fingerprint and remove the content. This is worth explaining to a teenager who is terrified of handing the picture to anyone.

keyAdvice.title: Report Remove is built for this
keyAdvice.body: In the UK, under-18s can use Report Remove, run jointly by Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation. The young person reports it themselves, verifies their age, and gets updates and counsellor support through their Childline account.

situations.context: Removal is rarely instant and rarely total. It is still worth doing, because every copy taken down is one fewer, and the services above are the only ones with direct removal channels into the major platforms.

countryNotes.CA: There is no separate Canadian removal service. Take It Down works here, and NeedHelpNow.ca has step-by-step removal instructions for each major platform.
countryNotes.IE: Intimate image abuse reports to Hotline.ie cannot be made anonymously, unlike their other report types.

situations.label: My child is being bullied or harassed
situations.summary: Sustained cruelty, exclusion, threats or humiliation, usually from people your child actually knows.

keyAdvice.title: Screenshot the pattern, not just the worst message
keyAdvice.body: A single message rarely gets acted on. A run of them over days does. Capture dates wherever you can.

keyAdvice.title: Report inside the platform first
keyAdvice.body: For bullying the platform genuinely is the right first stop, and most have a specific bullying or harassment category that routes faster than a general report.

keyAdvice.title: Involve the school if the people involved are from school
keyAdvice.body: Most online bullying between classmates is a school matter with an online surface. Schools have a duty here and are usually better placed to stop it than any platform is.

situations.context: Bullying is generally outside the remit of the child exploitation hotlines, which handle abuse and grooming. That is a routing decision rather than a brush-off, and the school plus the platform is the faster route.

countryNotes.UK: CEOP does not take bullying reports and will point you to Childline, which is the better service for it.

situations.label: They have seen something disturbing
situations.summary: Violent, sexual or otherwise upsetting content that has stayed with them.

keyAdvice.title: Deal with the child before the settings
keyAdvice.body: The instinct is to go and fix the controls. Do that later today. Right now the useful thing is letting them describe it, telling them it was not their fault for seeing it, and not reacting with alarm they then have to manage.

keyAdvice.title: If it was child sexual abuse material, do not screenshot it
keyAdvice.body: This is the one situation where screenshotting is the wrong move. Do not download, forward or save it. Report the address to your national body instead, using the reporting section above.

keyAdvice.title: Then tighten the setting that let it through
keyAdvice.body: Once they are settled, the relevant SafeStart guide has the specific control. It is usually a content maturity setting, a restricted mode, or an autoplay behaviour.

situations.context: Do not go looking for the content yourself to see how bad it was. If it is illegal material, viewing and saving it creates problems for you and for any investigation.

police.line: Hotlines are for reporting, not for emergencies. If someone is at risk right now, call first and report afterwards.
police.nonEmergency: For a non-emergency report, contact your local FBI field office, call 1-800-CALL-FBI, or use tips.fbi.gov.

bodies.name: NCMEC CyberTipline
bodies.what: The national reporting route for online child exploitation, grooming, and child sexual abuse material. Reports go to law enforcement.

bodies.name: Take It Down
bodies.what: Free removal service for intimate images taken of someone under 18. The image stays on your device.

bodies.name: NCMEC — get help now
bodies.what: Support hub, including help for families after a report.

bodies.name: FBI IC3
bodies.what: Intake for cyber-enabled crime. Useful for the record, but their own wording is that you will not be contacted by IC3. Do not rely on it for help in a live situation.

police.line: Hotlines are for reporting, not for emergencies. If someone is at risk right now, call first and report afterwards.
police.nonEmergency: Call 101 for a non-emergency report to your local police.

bodies.name: CEOP Safety Centre
bodies.what: Reports go to a Child Protection Advisor at CEOP, part of the National Crime Agency. For online sexual abuse or concerning contact from an adult. Not for bullying.

bodies.name: Report Remove
bodies.what: For under-18s in the UK to get a nude image of themselves taken down. Run by Childline with the Internet Watch Foundation.

bodies.name: Internet Watch Foundation
bodies.what: Anonymous reporting of child sexual abuse imagery, including AI-generated and drawn material, for removal.

bodies.name: NSPCC Helpline
bodies.what: For adults worried about a child. Free, and you do not have to give your name.
bodies.phone: 0808 800 5000 — phone 10am to 4pm Mon to Fri, email help@nspcc.org.uk 11am to 4pm daily
bodies.caveatNote: Not a 24-hour service. Childline, for your child rather than for you, is 24 hours on 0800 1111.

police.line: Hotlines are for reporting, not for emergencies. If someone is at risk right now, call first and report afterwards.
police.nonEmergency: Contact your local police service. Cybertip forwards its reports to police as well.

bodies.name: Cybertip.ca
bodies.what: Canada's national tipline, run by the Canadian Centre for Child Protection. Covers child sexual abuse material, grooming, luring, intimate images, sextortion and AI deepfakes.
bodies.phone: Staffed 8:30am to 4:00pm Central, Mon to Fri. Online reporting is open at all times.

bodies.name: NeedHelpNow.ca
bodies.what: For under-18s whose images are being shared. Has the clearest step-by-step removal instructions for Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Discord and others that we found anywhere.

bodies.name: Take It Down
bodies.what: The image removal service used by Canadian families, since there is no separate Canadian one. It works internationally.

police.line: Hotlines are for reporting, not for emergencies. If someone is at risk right now, call first and report afterwards.
police.nonEmergency: Your local Garda station. Garda Confidential is 1800 666 111, and the Garda child sexual abuse reporting line is 1800 555 222.

bodies.name: An Garda Síochána
bodies.what: The Irish police. Report directly to them. A hotline report does not replace it.
bodies.phone: 999 or 112 in an emergency, 1800 555 222 for child sexual abuse reporting

bodies.name: Hotline.ie
bodies.what: Reporting for child sexual abuse material, grooming, intimate image abuse and sexual extortion. Anonymous, except for intimate image abuse reports.

bodies.name: ISPCC Childline
bodies.what: 24-hour listening service for children and young people up to 18. For your child rather than for you.

bodies.name: Coimisiún na Meán
bodies.what: The media regulator. Use this when a platform has failed to act, not as a first step. You need to have reported to the platform first, and they will not accept child sexual abuse material.

platforms.name: Roblox
platforms.route: In app: the shield or Report icon in the menu, or the three dots on a profile, chat or item. As a parent you can also report from Parental Controls → Settings → Communications using your child's account.

platforms.name: Fortnite and Epic Games
platforms.route: In game, or the web form below. Epic has the clearest reporting route of any platform here.

platforms.name: Discord
platforms.route: Discord has a dedicated form for parents and guardians, which does not require you to be in the server. If you have access to your teen's account you can also report from inside the app.
platforms.urlLabel: Contacting Discord Safety as a parent

platforms.name: Snapchat
platforms.route: Press and hold on the content to report in app. Snapchat also has web forms, including one specifically for leaked nudity and sexual content.

platforms.name: Instagram
platforms.route: Reporting is in app. The help pages describe the process rather than offering a separate form, so you generally need access to the account to report content.

platforms.name: TikTok
platforms.route: Press and hold on the video, comment or message, then Report. We could not verify a working web reporting form, so in-app is the reliable route.

platforms.name: YouTube
platforms.route: Reporting requires you to be signed in to a Google account. There is no signed-out web reporting tool, so you will need to be on an account to report a video, channel or comment.

platforms.name: Minecraft
platforms.route: Use the in-game player reporting tool. We could not verify a web reporting form. For Microsoft accounts, the Xbox complaint route below also applies.

platforms.name: Xbox and Microsoft
platforms.route: File a complaint about a player through Xbox support.

platformsNote: Platform reporting routes move often, and several of these companies have deliberately pushed reporting inside the app and behind a login. Where we could not confirm a working web form we say so rather than guessing. If a link here fails, the in-app route described alongside it still works.

lines.text: You are not in trouble. I am glad you told me.
lines.note: Reassurance comes before every practical step, and it is the part most parents skip.

lines.text: This is not your fault, even if you made a choice you regret. What they are doing is a crime.
lines.note: Worth saying almost word for word.

lines.text: My first move is to help. Always.
lines.note: Children weigh up whether telling you will make things worse. This answers that before they ask.

lines.text: We are going to sort this out together, and I am not taking your phone away as a punishment for telling me.
lines.note: SafeStart's own addition. Fear of losing the device is one of the most common reasons children tell nobody.

standingLine: Reporting to a hotline does not replace reporting to the police. If your child is in immediate danger, call the emergency number first.
disclaimer: SafeStart is not an emergency service and cannot take reports. This page points you to the organizations that can. Every link and phone number here was checked against the organization's own website on the date shown.
